metric.why: Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing. Fleet utilization is where the money hides in most enterprise estates, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.
metric.definition: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.

reading.body:
Server utilization rate is the share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak. It is the denominator that makes every other efficiency metric honest.

The distinction between time and peak is the whole point. A fleet sized for its busiest hour looks fully committed on a capacity plan and mostly idle on a meter. Idle servers still draw power, still hold licenses, and still depreciate. Utilization is where that gap becomes visible, and it is the number that tells an operator whether the constraint is real demand or provisioning habit.

For AI specifically, the measurement is harder than the definition suggests. Training and inference workloads are bursty, and a rate averaged over time will understate what a cluster must be built to absorb. The data here does not resolve that tension. It defines the metric and places it in capacity and server use, alongside stranded power and space per cabinet and floor loading limits, which are the physical counterparts to the same question: how much of what you built is actually earning.

What this does not cover is any actual utilization figure, any target, or any comparison across operators. It is a definition and a placement, not a measurement.
